TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
THURSDAY, 10 NOVEMBER 2022 AT 10.01 AM (AEST)
DAY 11
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR TRENT GLOVER, for the Commonwealth
MR A VIAL, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes, Commissioner, I appear with Ms Marsh again today.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I appear with Mr Glover and Mr Vial for the
Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. And that's all the appearances for today or not?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: I believe so, yes.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: One housekeeping matter, Commissioner. On the list of potential witnesses
for this week or anticipated witnesses, Ms Annette Musolino was included on that list but
it's now clear she won't be reached this week, and it's expected that she will be called
during the second hearing block.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Commissioner, Mr Pratt is ready to give evidence.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Mr Pratt, will you take an oath or an affirmation?
MR PRATT: An affirmation, please.
<FINN AXEL PRATT, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY KC
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Thank you, Commissioner. Mr Pratt, could you tell the Commission
your name, please?
MR PRATT: Finn Axel Pratt.
MR GREGGERY: You received a notice to give evidence and produce documents numbered
NTG-0015 dated 6th October 2022.
MR PRATT: I did.
MR GREGGERY: And you produced a statement in response dated 18th October 2022.

MR PRATT: I did.
MR GREGGERY: And I gather that since 18th October, you have had the opportunity to look
for some diary notes and other documents that might be relevant and to which your
attention had been drawn?
MR PRATT: I have reviewed my diaries yet again, multiple times, and found a couple of extra
things.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. You included some attachments to your statement, and there
are other documents which have been identified as having potential relevance to your
evidence. Commissioner, I tender the exhibits in the draft list for day 11, which are currently
numbered 1222 through to 1235D.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Those exhibits will be admitted with the numbering in accordance
with the schedule.
<EXHIBITS 1222 TO 1235D AS PER THE SCHEDULE
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, might I just have it noted on the transcript that as per
the schedule, a series of those documents are tendered for the limited purpose, having
regard to the Parliamentary Privileges Act.
COMMISSIONER: Right.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: That's how -
COMMISSIONER: You have lost me, I'm sorry. Can you make that a bit clearer?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Sorry, Commissioner. We have been notified - the Commonwealth
have been notified that the - as per the exhibit list - - -
COMMISSIONER: Okay there are some things that might attract parliamentary privilege if
they were used to -- that sort of thing. Is that right?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: For a prohibited purpose that's right. Our understanding is they are not
intended to be used for any prohibited purpose and I'm just formally noting that. Thank you,
Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you. Yes, Mr Greggery
MR GREGGERY: Yes, thank you, Commissioner. There is one further issue. I'm told that
Exhibit number 1232 is in fact a duplicate, so I can fill the gap with a different document.
Which might put the document production people to a state of uncertainty, but if I hand up
these two.

MR GREGGERY: Yes. And substitution with Diary Entry, and the date is the 22nd of January
2015.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. The diary entry then will be 1232 and you have given me two
copies, one for the record, is it?
<EXHIBIT 1232 (AMENDED) DIARY ENTRY DATED 22/01/2015
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: Mr Pratt, apologies for the housekeeping in the middle of your evidence.
You are currently retired?
MR PRATT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: You were the former Secretary for the Department of Social Services for a
period?
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: You have set out your employment history, as it were, within the Australian
Public Service in your statement?
MR PRATT: I did.
MR GREGGERY: Relevant for the scope of this inquiry, you have extensive experience with
both the Department of Human Services, in some respects, but also the Department of
Social Services?
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: In September 2008, you were appointed to the Chief Executive Officer role
at Centrelink?
MR PRATT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And I understand that you remained in that role for almost a year through
to August 2009?
MR PRATT: Correct.
MR GREGGERY: And then were appointed as the Secretary of the Department of Human
Services in September 2009?

MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: That role continued for about a year and a half through to April 2011.
MR PRATT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: You were then the Secretary of the Department of Families, Housing,
Community Services and Indigenous Affairs. And that's been brought up on the screen now.
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And you can confirm that's what appears at paragraph 7 of your statement?
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: The period that is of particular significance to the Commission is, as you
understand, your role of Secretary of the Department of Social Services from September
2013 to September 2017.
MR PRATT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: During that period of time, I gather Ms Campbell was the Secretary of the
Department of Human Services?
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: That is, she took that role in about September 2013, to your knowledge?
MR PRATT: No, she moved into Human Services after I left in April 2011. She would have
been there probably March-April.
MR GREGGERY: Okay. Can we deal with things at a relatively high level first. Describe in your
own terms the role of the Department of Social Services from the perspective that you held,
that is, one of Secretary?
MR PRATT: Yes. The Department of Social Services was the social policy department for the
Commonwealth Government, and so we provided advice to governments over time on a
huge range of matters, including income support policies for all manner of vulnerable
Australians, families, pensioners, people looking for work, people with disabilities and so
forth. And in addition to that - and perhaps, Mr Greggery, it would be easier at some stage
to have a look at the list I have included in my statement of the range of responsibilities of
the Department during this period.
MR GREGGERY: Perhaps if paragraph 14 could be brought up on the screen.
MR PRATT: Yes, that's right.

MR GREGGERY: Certainly, yes.
MR PRATT: So, as you can see there, we are responsible for the welfare system or social
security system, looked after family services, carer services, a range of disability services
which include, of course, the National Disability Insurance Scheme. I worked on the NDIS for
six years. We had disability employment services, aged care, childcare, etcetera. You can see
it's a very long list of things. Another thing which we had during that period which was quite
prominent in terms of our work was the work we did around settlement services, which had
come over from Immigration in late 2013. Childcare joined the Department in - at Christmas
time 2014.
MR GREGGERY: Obviously a very large Department with enormous responsibility?
MR PRATT: I felt so, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And not just in terms of the areas, but also in terms of the extent of
financial measures under its implementation or supervision?
MR PRATT: So, DSS' budget at this time, and this is peak DSS, was probably about a third of
the entire expenditure of the Commonwealth at that time. $130 billion-plus a year.
MR GREGGERY: You describe in paragraph 14 - that's the introduction - the social policy
advice role of DSS. It included, as I understand it, the attachments to your statement, also a
responsibility for legislation that related to its various responsibilities in a social policy
sense?
MR PRATT: Yes, that's right. The Department of Social Services also was responsible for over
50 pieces of legislation during this period, which includes the Social Security Act and its
(Administration) Act and many others. Mr Greggery, it might be worthwhile just showing
that list.
MR GREGGERY: Yes, thank you. We can go - --
COMMISSIONER: I don't know that you need to help Mr Greggery a lot. He's been doing
fairly well so far. But thank you, Mr Pratt.
MR PRATT: Thank you, Commissioner.
MR GREGGERY: If we could go to what is described as Attachment A to your statement, it is
an Administrative Arrangements Order, Exhibit 1223, I'm told. Just while that's being
brought up, I might identify something which is perhaps obvious, but the events in respect
of your involvement with what became the Robodebt Scheme occurred, of course, in your
period as Secretary, and as you have identified, you had a vast range of responsibilities and
undoubtedly a vast range of people reporting to you. Are you able to independently - that is,
independently of documents - recall significant events about the scheme? Or is it the case
that the extent of your memory is largely confined to what exists in the documents?

MR PRATT: Certainly, my recollection of the Robodebt Scheme is as identified in the
documents. As I make a point, though, in my statement, I, inevitably, there would have been
other conversations and meetings and discussions I had with Ministers, my senior people,
the Secretary of the Department of Human Services, Kathryn Campbell. So my recollection
after - well, nearly eight years ago, through until five years ago when I left Social Services - is
reasonable, but it's not perfect. And so I acknowledge in my statement that they there
would have been other occasions when I actually had - inevitably had - involvement with Ms
Campbell, my senior people, Ministers during that time.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And during the period that you were the Secretary of the Department,
the Robodebt Scheme, as it's described in the Letters Patent, was the subject of significant
public interest and media interest, particularly in late 2016 and from that point forward.
MR PRATT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And the subject of other inquiries in which your Department was involved.
MR PRATT: Yes, that's right.
MR GREGGERY: And that undoubtedly triggered significant interest from the Ministers
associated with the portfolio?
MR PRATT: It did.
MR GREGGERY: Which included the Department. The attachment is now up on the screen.
The first page is the Administrative Arrangements Order, and you identify that this was
really part of the machinery of government which established Departments and roles and
delineation between various Departments in the Commonwealth Government?
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: An order by the Governor-General, effectively, as the Executive.
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And what you've included - this is, of course, dated 23rd December 2014 - as
matters to be dealt with by the Department of which you were the Secretary includes - is on
the next page. Matters dealt with is the top half of the page, for which, in broad terms, is
the policy responsibility, as I understand what you described earlier in your evidence at
paragraph 14.
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And of particular reference here is income support and participation policy
for people of working age at line 3.

MR GREGGERY: The first three. If we move, then, down to the legislation administered by
the Minister, that's the Minister of Social Services.
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: We can see that starts halfway down the page. That's in alphabetical order
and goes over to the following page. These are the 50 or so pieces of legislation that were
under administration by your Department?
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And of reference to - or relevance to - this inquiry, we see at the top of page
37, the second entry is the Data-matching Program (Assistance and Tax) Act of 1990. And
then in the lower half of the document, we see references to Social Security Act 1991, and
the Social Security (Administration) Act of 1999.
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: Now, could you describe, then, the relationship - having established that
very high-level framework - the relationship between the Department of Social Services, of
which you were the Secretary, and the Department of Human Services, of which Ms
Campbell was the Secretary?
MR PRATT: That's right. At a very high level, my Department and I were responsible for the
policy related to the legislation in front of you and as set out in the matters that the
Department was responsible for. And the Department of Human Services was responsible
for the delivery of many of the requirements of these Acts and the policies that were looked
after by DSS.
MR GREGGERY: That is, your Department set the policy and was responsible for the
legislative aspects of that policy? And DHS administered or implemented those policies and
was the service delivery agency?
MR PRATT: That's right, with one caveat. As described in the Department of Human Services
Administrative Orders, they were responsible also for service delivery policy.
MR GREGGERY: I see. That is, a subset of the overarching policy responsibility of DSS?
MR PRATT: Well, it was directly its responsibility as an independent Department of State.
MR GREGGERY: We heard evidence last week from Mr Brown of Victoria Legal Aid, who
described that an action seeking judicial review on various declarations in the case of
Masterton was initially commenced against the Secretary of the Department of Human
Services, apparently on the understanding that that person was the decision-maker for the
debt raised in respect of Ms Masterton under the Robodebt Scheme. But very quickly by

agreement, it was the Commonwealth of Australia who was substituted as the respondent
in that legal process.
Is it the case that despite DSS having responsibility for this legislation and legislative
decisions and legal issues obviously related to policy and the legislation, that there is a bit of
a blurry line between ultimately where the buck stops in terms of decisions made in the
implementation of the program which might be broader than DHS?
MR PRATT: Well, possibly, yes. There are some blurry lines there. I mean, again, as I say in
my statement, it is very difficult to find a demarcation but pure policy, as I express it, was a
responsibility of the Department of Social Services. Service delivery policy was, or
operational policy was the responsibility of the Department of Human Services. But finding
that demarcation point is difficult.
MR GREGGERY: Of particular or direct relevance, of course, is the development of policy in
respect of what became the Robodebt Scheme. Where was the demarcation there, from
your perspective of Secretary?
MR PRATT: Okay. So I think there are three components of that. One is I, as Secretary of
DSS, was responsible for the overarching policy in relation to debt and compliance, as set
out in the Social Security Act. I was responsible as a Secretary for DSS for the advice that my
Department gave the Department of Human Services on the proposal which would become
Robodebt, and the Department of Human Services was responsible for the service delivery
policy proposal which emerged in 2015 in the 2015 Budget, which became Robodebt.
MR GREGGERY: And merely because a service delivery proposal is developed as part of a
budget measure, I take it that DSS is not relieved of its ongoing policy responsibilities in
respect of the measure?
MR PRATT: In terms of its ownership of the overarching policy interests? No.
MR GREGGERY: That is, there is a continuing obligation on the part of DSS through the
Administrative Arrangements Orders that it will monitor the implementation of it and
ensure that it's consistent with its own policy obligations.
MR PRATT: No, not quite. The AAOs for the Department of Social Services make it very clear
that they are responsible for the monitoring of their actions. They are a separate
Department of state. They are independent from DSS in that respect. In fact, they are
independent from DSS in all respects. We are colleague Departments in the portfolio. I go
into it at length in my statement, that at different stages DHS had its own portfolio, or was
in the finance portfolio, but I think it is very important to understand that in no way,
including when I was Secretary of DHS, was DHS ever subordinate to the Department of
Social Services.
Right. They were colleague Departments that happened to be in the same portfolio at that
time. There is a lengthy history to why - how - it got to that point, which obviously I imagine

MR GREGGERY: What, then, in the hypothetical scenario where DSS becomes aware that the
manner in which DHS is implementing social security policy is inconsistent with its own
position in a policy sense?
MR PRATT: Yes, well, at that time, we should alert them to that fact.
MR GREGGERY: Would you alert your Minister as well?
MR PRATT: Potentially. It depends on the scale of the issue. If it was relatively small and was
easily fixable, then possibly not. If it was a significant issue, then we might take it up with
the Minister.
MR GREGGERY: And what about your own responsibility for advice to the Minister? Can you
describe that?
MR PRATT: Well under the Public Service Act, I am the principal policy adviser to my Minister
of the day.
MR GREGGERY: That suggests an obligation to raise matters of policy where the matters are
significant, even if they might relate to the implementation by DHS of a particular policy.
MR PRATT: Possibly. It depends on the matter because it may well be that DHS themselves
are already raising that matter with the Minister. And it would not make sense for me to
weigh in on another Department's responsibilities unless necessary.
MR GREGGERY: And the easy way to check whether another Department has raised it with
its Minister would be a conversation between you and Ms Campbell?
MR PRATT: That could be a way, yes.
MR GREGGERY: There may be other ways?
MR PRATT: Well, yes. In the context of Robodebt, the Minister raised it with me.
MR GREGGERY: And when do you recall that conversation happening?
MR PRATT: So my - it's firmly in my mind, it was around very close to Christmas, one side or
the other. Either 2016 or early 2017. I remember seeing the media reports about what
became known as Robodebt. It was obvious to me that this was in relation to a service
delivery matter that was being administered by the Department of Human Services. The
Minister at the same time rang me up - in a sense, Minister Porter, I think, was quite
focused on it because he was getting media calls not as Social Services Minister, but as the
Acting Human Services Minister because then Minister Tudge who was the Human Services
Minister was on leave and Minister Porter was acting down for him at that time.

COMMISSIONER: You say, "acting down". Does that imply a senior/junior Minister
relationship?
MR PRATT: Yes, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Even though the Departments are seen as equal?
MR PRATT: That's right, Commissioner. So the - he would have been both Minister for Social
Services and Minister for Human Services at that time while Mr Tudge was on leave. But
Minister Tudge was a Minister. Minister Porter was a cabinet Minister who represented the
interests of the portfolio. Minister Tudge reported to Minister Porter.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
MR GREGGERY: Just dealing with that question of the respective relationship between the
two Departments, as part of your responsibilities as Secretary, annual reports were
prepared and signed under your hand?
MR PRATT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: You finished, as you said, in your role as Secretary of the Department in
about August or September 2017.
MR PRATT: September 2017, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And the Annual Report for the '16-17 financial year was released at that
point or slightly afterwards?
MR PRATT: Yes, I recall being happy that I was able to sign off the last of my annual reports
for the Department of Social Services.
MR GREGGERY: There is a passage in the report that I will read to you. I appreciate you don't
have it with you. I have provided it, of course, to my learned friend Ms Hogan-Doran, but I
will read it out and then ask for your comment about the question of the respective
relationship. Under the heading - it's page 92 of the report, under the heading Social
Security Debt-Raising and Recovery:
"Social security payments can be overpaid if the information held by DHS about recipients'
circumstances is incorrect. These overpayments can be due to recipient error (inadvertent or
deliberate), administrative error or a combination of these errors. Our debt identification
and recovery is managed by DHS, and we monitor and oversee this process. This year, DHS
raised 1,532,719 DSS debts valued at 1.5 billion and recovered 0.96 billion. A further 0.09
billion was waived. These figures include compensation debts but exclude family tax benefit
reconciliation and tax return non-lodger debts.”
Over to page 93:

"Debts were recovered through a variety of methods, with the primary method being
withholding of a portion of the current entitlement for recipients. We can waive our right to
recover the debt under certain conditions. These include cases where the debtor is subject to
extreme and unusual circumstances that interfere with their capacity to repay; the debt was
solely due to administrative error; that it is likely to be less than $50 in value and therefore
not cost effective to pursue. Indicators that are agreed with DHS measure the overall
effectiveness of debt management relating to social security program payments.”
The phrase that your debt - that is, DHS debt identification and recovery is managed by DHS
suggests some demarcation in the role but still almost a supervisory role?
MR PRATT: Yes. The reference to monitoring there, and the ANAO pointed out a failing we
had in that space earlier in the year. We did have a role - or I assume they still do - in
monitoring the actual achievement of measures in terms of debts recovered, the amount of
money that was recovered by the debt management operations of the Department of
Human Services.
MR GREGGERY: That is, there is an area of financial responsibility or monitoring of what
flows from DHS implementation and service delivery?
MR PRATT: Yes, that's right.
MR GREGGERY: That tends to suggest a degree of awareness also, that passage I read out,
about the manner in which debts were being recovered at the time.
MR PRATT: I think that's fair to say.
MR GREGGERY: And income averaging or its use in debt creation was the subject of the
media interest that occurred in December 2016 and January 2017.
MR PRATT: Well, that is one of the major flaws of the Robodebt Scheme, of course.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. But insofar as it was a flaw in the public arena, it was in the public
arena by reason of media interest late '16, early '17?
MR PRATT: Well, I don't actually recall that. The media that I focused on, as a former
Secretary of Human Services and CEO of Centrelink was, in fact, in relation to what I thought
was unusual administrative or operational arrangements for dealing with the people who
had potential debts. For example, I was quite surprised, for example, that the letters that
went to people didn't have telephone numbers on them. I mean, that is typically a better
practice, service delivery-wise.
Also there were many complaints about people not getting letters. That is reasonably
anticipatable based on the fact that the people that we are dealing with often move around
a lot. If they have stopped receipt of payment, they - I don't believe are still required to
advise of their current address to the government. So my focus was in those areas. I must

confess, I did not have a real consciousness or understanding of income averaging. It's not
something I had been exposed to before. I don't recall seeing that in the media.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. Just to be clear about the context in which you gave your answer in
respect of telephone numbers and people moving addresses and the like, that is, those were
matters of interest to you in late '16, early '17 from media inquiries by reason of your
experience - previous experience with Centrelink.
MR PRATT: That was my takeaway from those. And I should note, to be fair to Human
Services they did change those things pretty quickly.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask you, as DHS Secretary, were you aware of averaging ever
being used as a means of determining and raising debt?
MR PRATT: No, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Right. Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: The question of putting a telephone number on a letter seemed to be fairly
well settled in terms of point of contact, from your experience in DHS and CEO of
Centrelink?
MR PRATT: Certainly in my experience. As human Services Secretary and even when I was at
Centrelink, there was always an interest in seeing what functions could actually be moved
onto the computer system or could be automated in order to try and free up resources to
deal with the more difficult issues that customers faced. And so there - it was always that
incentive. When one is dealing with a complex matter like debt issues, and I'm no expert in
debt management or policy, but these are times where it does make sense to ensure that
you've got a human being who can actually talk to someone and help guide them through
the process.
MR GREGGERY: The scheme - that is, the size of the scheme as you have described it, even
in the '16-17 financial year, suggested that there was a very high degree of automation
about the raising and recovery of debts.
MR PRATT: Certainly the media - well, I think the Robodebt description was coined pretty
early in the sense. So, yes, there was clearly a heavy reliance on automation.
MR GREGGERY: And from your experience as Secretary of DHS in broad terms - and I
appreciate it's a decade ago now - but the level of debt interventions and recovery
processes was in the vicinity of 20,000 or so per year?
MR PRATT: I recall when I was at Centrelink, when I was first introduced to the concept of
data-matching between our then records, what recipients would report on in terms of their

saying, and I do recall thinking, oh, that's quite a clever thing to do. But I do recall that it was
quite small-scale, and my vague recollection was that it was pretty labour-intensive to do it.
MR GREGGERY: That is, it was used, as I understand it - correct me if I am wrong - from your
knowledge, as a starting point to identify potential discrepancies which would be
investigated using the traditional methods of compulsory obtaining of third-party
information in fairly labour-intensive way.
MR PRATT: I hate to confess, but your now knowledge on this has exceeded my then
knowledge of, it but absolutely.
MR GREGGERY: Okay. Coming back then to late 2016, early 2017, were you aware either
from the media or from your conversation with Minister Porter or any other conversations
you had at the time about the interest from ACOSS, the Australian Council of Social
Services?
MR PRATT: No.
MR GREGGERY: No. Alright. The conversation you had, then, when Minister Porter raised
the issue with you, can you take us through that in as much detail as you can recall?
MR PRATT: If I paraphrase, I seem to recall that Minister Porter might have said something
in the order of, "What the hell is this all about?” I think my response was, "You are reading
the same media I am. This is clearly something which DHS is doing." And in some fashion, I
connected Minister Porter as Acting Human Services Minister with whomever was acting for
Ms Campbell at the time as the Secretary of Human Services to ensure he received the
proper advice around what it was about, what was happening, how to handle the media.
MR GREGGERY: Do you recall any ongoing involvement again in relationship to the
connection you established between Minister Porter and the Acting Secretary of DHS?
MR PRATT: No, I don't. And certainly my records don't suggest that I did have further
involvement of that sort. But having said that, Mr Greggery, inevitably in meetings with the
Minister, he might have raised things to do with it. So I don't recall that being the case, but I
certainly assume that, being a topical issue, it would have come up.
MR GREGGERY: And in addition to the media interest, as you've identified, there were other
investigations and inquiries undertaken in respect of the issue, one of which was the
Ombudsman's inquiry.
MR PRATT: Well, the first one - and I got briefing on this in mid-January - was that the ANAO
was examining the combined effort of Human Services and DSS and our respective roles in
relation to previous debt compliance programs which pre-existed 2015-16. Sorry, '16-17.
And obviously the Auditor-General would have written to me ahead of that so I would have
known that we were contributing on that. But I became aware of that and then, yes, you are
right, the Ombudsman was also doing an inquiry into - what became known as the

MR GREGGERY: Do you recall being briefed by Serena Wilson about that time in respect of
questions of the legality of the scheme?
MR PRATT: No, I don't. But if Ms Wilson - I mean, it is quite likely that Ms Wilson would have
mentioned something to me. Sorry, let me rephrase that. I'm sure Ms Wilson would have
talked to me about the issues in relation to the scheme. I don't recall any discussion about
legalities or issues of that sort. But I'm not ruling it out.
MR GREGGERY: I understand. Perhaps if we could return back to broader questions and the
nature of your role and interaction with Ministers and go to paragraph 17 of your
statement. While that's being brought up, Mr Pratt, the size of the Department and the
various reports that you had to receive from branches and divisions, Deputy Secretaries and
the like, meant that really only the matters of high-level significance were drawn to your
attention?
MR PRATT: As a general rule, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And your role, as you describe it here in paragraph 17, included what is
understood traditionally as a CEO role. Principal policy advisor, as you say, and steward of
the APS. Frequent attendee at Cabinet committees, in particular the Expenditure Review
Committee which examined expenditure and savings proposals for the budget. And you say
there in 2015, DSS had 47 measures announced in that year's budget - more than half,
again, from the next largest department - and your attendance at Parliament was a regular
feature as well. The nature of the conversation, that you describe, in your recollection, with
Minister Porter appeared to indicate a level of comfort in frank dialogue between the two of
you.
MR PRATT: I accept that. Certainly Minister Porter felt comfortable having frank dialogue
with me.
MR GREGGERY: And what about his predecessor, Minister Morrison?
MR PRATT: Likewise. Likewise. I - my characterisation of my relationship with my Ministers
were they were open and positive, and, on occasion, there would be some disagreements or
some concern from the Minister at the time about actions of the Department or non-actions
and the like, or the quality of briefs or - on rare occasions - happily, where we had made a
mistake or something of that sort. But, yes, all of the cabinet Ministers I dealt with, in fact,
whenever I dealt with the Human Services Ministers during that period were positive and I
had as much opportunity as I needed to talk to them.
MR GREGGERY: Were there regular meetings scheduled in your diary between yourself and
Ministers?
MR PRATT: There were certainly very regular meetings. They moved around quite a lot
because the, of course, Ministers would travel a lot and their Parliamentary schedules

MR GREGGERY: If we were interested to look for where the content of those meetings was
documented, as opposed to having to rely on fading memories, given the passage of time,
